findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the failure behavior of the post-apply re-GET (retry/backoff, or skip-baseline-advance-for-that-field with a surfaced warning) so a failed GET does not silently regress to the stale start-of-pass baseline.
evidence: 'we re-GET the post-push canonical value and merge it into ctx.curr_snapshot'
ABSENCE: no error/timeout/retry handling described for the post-apply re-GET
findings.finding: The observe-after-push design adds an extra live GET in _apply_mutations for each mutated Jira key ('one extra GET, only on a changed field'). The plan does not specify what happens if that GET fails or times out. On failure, curr_snapshot is not merged, so the single _advance_baselines records the stale start-of-pass value, and the next pass will misread Jira's re-canonicalization as a human edit — exactly the failure the design exists to prevent.
scenarios: Jira API is slow or returns an error on the post-push GET after a successful update
findings.suggested_fix: On re-GET failure, skip merging that key (leave prior baseline), log/metric the miss, and treat the next pass conservatively rather than advancing to a possibly-stale value.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the failure behavior of the post-push observe GET (abort that field's baseline advance / retry / leave the field un-baselined) so a failed re-GET never lets the persist-phase advance record the stale start-of-pass value.
evidence: Plan: 'The baseline must be the value Jira holds AFTER our push, not the start-of-pass snapshot — a benign Jira re-canonicalization ... would otherwise be misread next pass as a human edit.'

reconcile.py:600-605: `_advance_baselines` is wrapped fail-open and unconditionally reads `ctx.curr_snapshot[jira_key]`; if the merge silently no-ops, the start-of-pass value persists as the baseline.
The plan does not say whether a failed post-push GET aborts the field's advance, retries, or falls back.
findings.finding: The observe-after-push extra GET has no stated failure/degradation handling; because the single `_advance_baselines` is fail-open and reads `ctx.curr_snapshot`, a silently-failed GET leaves the start-of-pass value in the snapshot and the always-on advance then records the stale pre-push value — reproducing the exact re-canonicalization misread the plan sets out to prevent.
scenarios: Jira re-canonicalizes rich ADF/wiki on write; the post-push GET times out; next pass sees remote != (stale) baseline and misreads it as a human edit.

But by the time rollback happens, Jira already holds rich ADF/wiki bodies written by the new path. The plan does not specify what the reconciler does with already-migrated rich data on rollback (re-plain-encode everything → churn, or leave it → baseline/local mismatch loop). The reversibility mechanism restores the code path but not the data state.

The plan does not state that the convergence/echo tests exercise a re-canonicalizing response (live or a fixture that alters the posted value); a mock echoing the posted bytes verbatim would pass while never exercising the re-canonicalization path.

evidence: Plan: 'The baseline must be the value Jira holds AFTER our push' — baselines are rewritten to rich-canonical form during cutover.

This matches the post-rollback applicability condition: 'changes how existing persisted records are interpreted'.

scenarios: Cutover enabled, several descriptions re-emit and their baselines are rewritten to rich-canonical ADF/wiki; a bad rollout flips the flag off; next pass compares the rich-canonical baseline against a plain-normalized remote and sees a false divergence, re-syncing (echoing) a body that never changed.
findings.suggested_fix: Add an AC/test (e.g. `test_cutover_rollback_baseline_reconverges`) that enables the cutover, lets a description re-emit and rewrite its baseline to rich form, flips the flag off, then asserts the next plain-path pass either re-canonicalizes the stored baseline to plain form once and converges (zero further updates) or otherwise ignores the residual `rich_sha` — proving no spurious re-sync or clobber survives the revert.
